alt_text: Retained concrete bunker walls surround a shallow pool crossed by a narrow platform at Duisburg-Nord.
caption: Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord: retained ore-bunker walls frame water and a new crossing. The closer view makes adaptation of the industrial ground visible. Landscape adaptation by Latz + Partner.

alt_text: A shaded pavilion and arcaded gallery face the bright open Court of the Lions at the Alhambra.
caption: Court of the Lions, Alhambra. Covered edges offer a different exposure from the open court; this view illustrates a choice of sun and shelter, without establishing orientation or seasonal temperatures. Nasrid royal workshop under Muhammad V.
existing_heading: The Court of the Lions, Alhambra

alt_text: An unplanted excavated drainage basin in front of a planted bioswale beside buildings and a path.
caption: Two bioswales at different stages: the excavated foreground makes the receiving landform visible, while planting occupies the completed bed beyond. Storage, soil and overflow still need project-specific verification.
heading: Bioswales in construction and use
text: These photographs show real planted drainage spaces rather than a proposed school scheme. Read the depression and its position among hard surfaces before looking at the planting. Their different stages make the constructed ground easier to understand; neither photograph establishes measured runoff performance.

alt_text: A rectangular planted street bed sits beside a Brooklyn pavement and a row of blue rental bicycles.
caption: Dean Street, Brooklyn: a planted bioswale occupies the street edge beside cycle parking. Its everyday urban setting shows drainage as part of public space rather than an isolated landscape object.

alt_text: A continuous curved terrace at Royal Crescent faces an open green lawn with a clear building edge.
caption: Royal Crescent, Bath. The continuous curved frontage gives the open lawn a recognizable edge while leaving a broad outward connection. John Wood the Younger.

alt_text: A vaulted street portico in Bologna has a long clear walking line beside doors and an open square.
caption: Portico di Santo Stefano, Bologna. The sheltered route meets doors and an open public space, showing how an arcade belongs to everyday street life.

alt_text: Broad stone steps cross the lower courtyard toward a recessed arched doorway at Haddon Hall.
caption: Haddon Hall: courtyard, steps and a recessed doorway form successive arrival spaces. This historic sequence is a spatial comparison; the stairs are not a model for inclusive access.
heading: Haddon Hall — a historic arrival sequence
text: The lower courtyard provides a second real comparison: approach takes place within an outdoor room before reaching a recessed doorway. The photograph makes depth and successive thresholds visible. A contemporary entrance needs to achieve that legibility alongside an equally clear step-free approach.

alt_text: Bologna street portico with columns toward the square and entrances along the sheltered inside edge.
caption: Bologna, Santo Stefano. Columns, doorways and the adjoining square give the building edge depth: a person can move along it, enter through it or pause beside it.

alt_text: Two parallel concrete building ranges at the Salk Institute flank a courtyard opening toward the ocean.
caption: Salk Institute: separate ranges put long building faces beside open sky. The view explains a massing relationship; it does not establish internal room depths or daylight levels. Louis I. Kahn.
heading: The Salk Institute — a massing comparison
text: The two ranges beside the Salk courtyard offer another real way to read building form and exposed faces together. Open space separates the ranges instead of being left only around an undifferentiated block. Compare this visible arrangement with the diagram, while keeping room-level daylight questions separate.

alt_text: The Salk Institute court lies between concrete building ranges and opens to the Pacific at its far end.
caption: Salk Institute: the long court is strongly framed at its sides and open toward the ocean. It contrasts with the Alhambra’s more enclosed, sheltered perimeter; enclosure alone does not establish everyday occupation. Louis I. Kahn.
heading: The Salk Institute — an open-ended court
text: This real courtyard provides a useful contrast to the Alhambra. Its parallel edges establish a clear outdoor room, while the far end remains visually open. The photograph invites questions about exposure, routes and places to stay rather than proving that a monumental court is comfortable for every daily activity.

alt_text: A continuous row of brick terraced houses on Wynyatt Street shares side walls along a London pavement.
caption: Wynyatt Street, London: adjoining houses make the shared-wall principle visible. The street photograph does not reveal the terrace’s rear form, insulation or measured energy use.
heading: A London terrace — shared walls made visible
text: The real terrace on Wynyatt Street helps ground the housing comparison in an observable street form. A continuous frontage replaces the side gaps between detached houses. Establishing an actual surface-to-floor ratio would still require plans and sections; the photograph shows the arrangement, not its calculated performance.

alt_text: Timber frames and open sliding screens reveal a sequence of tatami rooms at Katsura Imperial Villa.
caption: Katsura Imperial Villa: framed openings and sliding screens make successive rooms legible. The image shows adjustable thresholds; it does not establish who historically had access to each room.
heading: Katsura — successive room thresholds
text: In this real interior, rooms remain visually connected through several framed openings, while sliding screens offer ways to change that connection. It is a comparison for degrees of exposure and enclosure. Contemporary privacy arrangements should follow the people and activities involved rather than reproduce a historic social hierarchy.

alt_text: An entrance stair at Stockholm Public Library rises through a darker passage toward the bright circular book hall.
caption: Stockholm Public Library: the approach reveals the central book hall as a shared destination. The contrast of compressed route and open room makes the heart recognizable, while raising separate questions about inclusive arrival. Gunnar Asplund.

alt_text: Open sliding panels link adjoining tatami rooms within timber frames at Katsura Imperial Villa.
caption: Katsura Imperial Villa: open sliding screens connect adjoining rooms while their frames retain each room’s identity. The view shows spatial linkage, not a tested modern acoustic partition.
heading: Katsura — rooms linked by sliding screens
text: This real interior shows rooms joining through wide framed openings with sliding panels. The opening can change the relationship without erasing each room’s proportions. Use it to study linkage and threshold depth; acoustic privacy, fire separation and accessible operation require contemporary solutions.

alt_text: A broad stair curves beside the circular Reading Room in the British Museum Great Court under a glazed roof.
caption: British Museum Great Court: the stair keeps the Reading Room in view as a stable reference during movement. The photograph shows a local spatial cue, not a complete assessment of museum wayfinding. Great Court redesign by Foster and Partners.

alt_text: The west entrance of Tate Modern is visible at the base of the brick power station beside its outside forecourt.
caption: Tate Modern’s west entrance. A broad arrival space meets the retained power-station shell, giving the main public entry a setting beyond the door itself. Power station by Giles Gilbert Scott; conversion by Herzog & de Meuron.

alt_text: Visitors move down the broad entrance ramp into Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall alongside its retained industrial walls.
caption: Tate Modern: the broad ramp brings visitors into the principal hall through a shared spatial experience. The photograph illustrates the route relationship; it does not verify gradients, surfaces or compliance. Conversion by Herzog & de Meuron.
heading: Tate Modern — a shared arrival route
text: The entrance ramp offers a real comparison for arrival as a shared journey into the main space. Visitors remain together in a generous volume instead of dividing immediately between a ceremonial stair and a concealed secondary entrance. The visible relationship is useful even though technical access performance cannot be assessed from the photograph.

alt_text: A stair rises between dark walls toward the illuminated circular book hall at Stockholm Public Library.
caption: Stockholm Public Library: ascent culminates in the bright book hall. The stair stages a change of enclosure and view; contemporary access needs an equally dignified alternative to steps. Gunnar Asplund.

alt_text: The Great Court stair wraps around the Reading Room with an open landing visible from the museum court.
caption: British Museum Great Court: the stair and landing are visible within the shared room. Movement contributes to the room’s activity while the destination remains legible. Great Court redesign by Foster and Partners.
heading: The British Museum — a stair within the shared room
text: This real stair remains part of the court rather than disappearing into an enclosed corridor. Its relationship to the Reading Room gives movement a stable background and makes the upper destination visible. Study that shared-space relationship together with the museum’s other routes, not as a reason to make stairs the only prominent choice.

alt_text: Individual timber study desks and chairs sit beside tall windows at Phillips Exeter Academy Library.
caption: Phillips Exeter Academy Library: desks, chairs, side screens and adjacent glazing make the individual window carrel directly visible. This is the occupied edge discussed here, rather than the central-hall context view. Louis I. Kahn.

alt_text: A smaller reading area with a table and shelves sits through an arch off the larger Furness Library interior.
caption: Furness Library, University of Pennsylvania: an arched opening gives a smaller reading area its own enclosure while keeping it connected to the larger interior. Frank Furness; later restoration by Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates.
heading: Furness Library — a smaller room at the edge
text: This real reading area makes the room-within-a-room relationship visible. A broad opening maintains connection, while the lower, framed enclosure identifies a distinct place to sit. The photograph supports a spatial reading; it does not establish sound isolation or current accessibility.

alt_text: The Kimbell gallery’s concrete vault and lower side edge make different overhead conditions visible above artworks.
caption: Kimbell Art Museum: the vaulted gallery offers a different overhead scale from the Pantheon. Compare ceiling shape and the relation to occupation rather than copying either building’s dimensions. Louis I. Kahn.
heading: The Kimbell — overhead form at gallery scale
text: The gallery provides a real comparison at a more closely occupied scale. Its curved overhead surface is legible above people, furnishings and display walls. Reading it beside the Pantheon helps separate the effect of overhead form from the idea that every important room must be exceptionally tall.

alt_text: Seating and a table inside the Farnsworth House face full-height glazing overlooking grass and trees.
caption: Farnsworth House: views of the surrounding landscape remain available from the occupied interior. The openness also makes privacy and solar exposure part of the same design question. Ludwig Mies van der Rohe for Dr. Edith Farnsworth.
heading: Farnsworth House — outlook from an occupied room
text: The real interior places everyday furniture beside broad views of trees and ground. The useful observation is the connection from a place to sit into a larger landscape. Its extensive glazing also invites a critical reading: outlook, exposure, privacy and seasonal comfort need to be considered together.

alt_text: Armchairs sit against the walls of a small windowed reading corner at Randall Library in Stow, Massachusetts.
caption: Randall Library, Stow: chairs occupy a smaller corner with protected sides and daylight. The visible enclosure offers a choice within the library; the image alone cannot establish acoustic privacy.
heading: Two library edges — places with protected sides
text: These real library interiors show different degrees of enclosure. Randall Library uses a small windowed corner; the Furness Library view frames a reading area through an arch. Both make a distinct place at the edge of a larger setting without demonstrating that every user will prefer it.

alt_text: A Furness Library reading area is framed by an arch and enclosing walls with bookshelves and a table.
caption: Furness Library: the arched threshold and surrounding walls give the table a protected setting while preserving a connection to the larger room. Frank Furness; later restoration by Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates.
existing_heading: Two library edges — places with protected sides

alt_text: Two Gothic windows meet on adjoining walls beside a chair in a blue room at Strawberry Hill House.
caption: Strawberry Hill House: windows on adjoining walls make two directions of daylight directly visible. The photograph illustrates the arrangement; exposure settings cannot establish measured brightness balance. House developed by Horace Walpole and collaborators.
heading: Strawberry Hill — windows around a corner
text: This real corner room supplies a literal two-sided-light example alongside the Kimbell’s rooflight comparison. Openings meet on adjacent walls, making the possible directions of light easy to read. Window size, orientation, obstructions and interior finishes still determine how well that arrangement works through the day.

alt_text: Green external louvred shutters stand open on some windows and closed across others on a Genoa facade.
caption: Genoa: external louvred shutters are visible in both open and closed positions. The comparison shows adjustable interception outside the glazing without establishing a measured cooling benefit.
heading: Genoa — adjustable shutters outside the glass
text: The real facade shows the same family of openings with shutters in different positions. This makes shading a usable component rather than a fixed diagram of the sun. Maintenance, safe operation, view and the needs of each room affect whether occupants can use such a system effectively.

alt_text: Two photographs compare a jalousie window with its glass louvres closed and tilted open.
caption: A jalousie window, closed and open. The change in free opening is directly visible; a second opening, a suitable pressure difference and an unobstructed room path are still needed for cross-ventilation.
heading: An operable louvre window — the controllable opening
text: This real component comparison shows one part of the ventilation path changing state. It is useful because a drawn opening is only effective when someone can actually operate it. The photograph does not show a complete cross-ventilated room or demonstrate adequate airflow under any particular weather condition.

alt_text: Exposed facade insulation and unfinished protective layers surround a window during a department-store retrofit.
caption: Facade insulation during retrofit. The window perimeter shows where continuous layers must be coordinated with an opening. This is a construction-stage observation, not an endorsed junction detail.
heading: A facade retrofit — continuity at an opening
text: This real construction photograph exposes insulation and unfinished layers around a window. It makes the interface visible in a way that a finished facade cannot. Compare the installation with the conceptual sections, while recognizing that the photograph cannot verify airtightness, fire provisions or the completed thermal bridge treatment.

alt_text: The open upper floor of Crown Hall has repeated perimeter glazing and a broad ceiling above low internal partitions.
caption: Crown Hall: repeated perimeter modules sit beside a broad, open interior and low partitions. The photograph connects a visible building rhythm with occupation, without supplying structural calculations. Ludwig Mies van der Rohe with Pace Architects and C.F. Murphy Associates.
heading: Crown Hall — perimeter rhythm and an open interior
text: This real interior complements the Fagus exterior view. Repeated perimeter modules provide a readable order, while low elements organize occupation within the larger room. A photograph cannot identify every load path or establish the freedom of future alterations; drawings and engineering records remain necessary.

alt_text: An unfinished ventilated facade exposes insulation, a membrane, metal supports and partly installed outer panels.
caption: Ventilated-facade installation: insulation, membrane, supports and outer panels can be distinguished before closure. The image does not establish cavity dimensions, drainage completion or fire stopping.
heading: An exposed facade assembly — layers before closure
text: The real installation photograph helps distinguish the outer cladding from the layers behind it. Read the supports and the separation between components before returning to the water-path diagram. Several critical junctions remain outside the frame, so it should not be used as a complete construction specification.

alt_text: A close view shows bolts joining a galvanized steel floor joist to another steel member at a building edge.
caption: Bolted steel floor connection, Stone County, Missouri. The fastener heads make the joining method visible; safe removal, loading and later access still require project-specific assessment.
heading: A bolted floor connection — a visible joining method
text: This real detail complements the Salk conservation example by exposing a connection rather than only a finished assembly. The fasteners can be identified and discussed as separate parts. Visibility at this construction stage does not prove that they remain accessible after finishes or that removal is safe without temporary support.

alt_text: Existing ore-bunker walls at Duisburg-Nord enclose water and a new narrow crossing for visitors.
caption: Duisburg-Nord: industrial walls are retained as the setting for a new landscape experience. Reuse operates at the scale of ground and enclosure as well as the scale of an entire building. Landscape adaptation by Latz + Partner.
heading: Duisburg-Nord — retaining an industrial enclosure
text: The adapted ore bunkers offer a real comparison at a smaller scale than Tate Modern’s hall. Existing walls give the new landscape a spatial structure that replacement would have erased. The image demonstrates the retained enclosure; investigation, remediation and maintenance decisions remain essential parts of any such reuse.

alt_text: External service towers, ducts and glazed circulation rise beside the main volume of the Lloyd’s Building in London.
caption: Lloyd’s Building, London: service towers and circulation are visibly distinguished from the principal occupied volume. The separation is legible, but the photograph cannot prove ease of replacement. Richard Rogers Partnership.
heading: Lloyd’s Building — services made legible
text: This real exterior makes several building systems readable as distinct components rather than concealing them behind one uniform skin. It is a useful comparison for thinking about layers and access. Visible separation is only a starting point: connection details, maintenance routes and replacement sequences determine actual adaptability.

alt_text: Accessible bolt heads connect galvanized steel members in an exposed floor assembly before finishes are installed.
caption: Bolted steel connection: identifiable fasteners offer a starting point for planning separation. A reversible-looking joint alone does not establish a safe disassembly sequence or a viable next use.
heading: A bolted assembly — one part of a removal sequence
text: This real construction detail makes the joining method inspectable. It invites concrete questions about which fasteners must be reached, which member needs support first and what finishes might later hide the connection. The image illustrates a component-level opportunity, not proof that the complete building was designed for disassembly.

alt_text: A worn route through winter grass and patchy snow crosses an open green toward a bridge in Cambridge.
caption: A winter desire line in Cambridge: repeated movement leaves a visible trace across the ground. It is evidence to investigate alongside access needs and interviews, rather than an instruction to pave every worn line.
heading: A desire line — behavior leaving a trace
text: The real ground trace gives observation a visible starting point. People have repeatedly crossed here, but the photograph alone cannot explain their destinations, the seasonality of the route or who finds it difficult to use. A useful brief would connect that trace with repeated observation and conversations before proposing an intervention.

alt_text: The curved frontage of Royal Crescent frames a broad lawn with a continuous built edge.
caption: Royal Crescent: a continuous curved frontage is one observable way to frame open space. Use it as a spatial reference, not as evidence of a competition between the projects shown here. John Wood the Younger.
heading: Built forms as references for a comparison
text: Photographs of a continuous terrace and a composition of differentiated building wings can help a team name the relationships it wants to test. These are real references, not alternatives developed for the same brief. The next step is to draw comparable proposals with consistent area, access and environmental assumptions rather than select a favorite photograph.

alt_text: The Bauhaus workshop wing and connecting building elements show differentiated volumes rather than a continuous housing frontage.
caption: Bauhaus, Dessau: differentiated volumes offer a contrasting massing reference. The comparison concerns spatial relationships; different programs and sites prevent a direct performance ranking. Walter Gropius.
existing_heading: Built forms as references for a comparison

alt_text: A historic photograph shows a full-size column capital and portico ceiling mock-up standing within timber scaffolding.
caption: Washington State Capitol, Olympia, 1926: a full-size plaster column and ceiling mock-up makes overhead geometry inspectable before final construction. Historic architectural mock-up, not a contemporary access test. Architects Wilder and White.
heading: Two real mock-ups — geometry and materials
text: These photographs show two different questions being brought out of drawings. The historic plaster assembly makes a column-and-ceiling relationship tangible at building scale. The brick panel places actual materials and joints together. Neither substitutes for a task-based reception or classroom trial, but both show why a physical test needs a clear question.

alt_text: A freestanding brick sample panel displays several bands of different brick colors and mortar arrangements.
caption: A brick mock-up panel places materials, joints and color combinations side by side at actual size. It supports a material decision; a spatial usability question needs a different kind of full-scale test.
existing_heading: Two real mock-ups — geometry and materials

alt_text: The BedZED power-house building stands beside a road and parked cars with its glazed entrance and roof form visible.
caption: BedZED’s power house: a building-services photograph makes one subject of operational follow-up tangible. Published evaluation, rather than the appearance of the plant building, establishes how systems performed. BedZED by Bill Dunster Architects and the project team.

alt_text: Homes and shared outdoor circulation at BedZED show the occupied development discussed in its published follow-up reporting.
caption: BedZED: the occupied housing setting belongs alongside the services when considering performance and everyday use. The photograph supplies context for the cited reporting, not measured results. Bill Dunster Architects and the project team.
